nameStory: Rose Coreopsis gets its name from its unusual pink or white petals that look like tiny roses compared to its bright yellow cousins. The "coreopsis" part comes from Greek words meaning "bug-like," referring to the seeds that supposedly look like little ticks - which is why the whole genus is nicknamed "tickseed." It's quite the rebel in the tickseed family, trading the typical sunny yellow for soft, rosy hues!
description: Rose Coreopsis is a delicate wildflower that breaks all the rules for its family by sporting pink or white petals instead of the usual bright yellow. This charming little plant produces daisy-like flowers with soft-colored petals surrounding a cheerful yellow center. It's a low-growing perennial that loves to get its feet wet, thriving in marshes and boggy areas where many other wildflowers can't survive. The plant has a somewhat sprawling habit and creates lovely drifts of pastel blooms in late summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small daisy-like flowers with 8 pink or white petals (ray florets) surrounding a bright yellow center - completely unlike the yellow flowers of other tickseeds. The petals feel papery and delicate to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, thread-like leaves that are opposite each other on the stem and feel smooth when rubbed between your fingers. They're much finer than most wildflower leaves and almost grass-like in appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading plant that forms loose colonies in wet areas. The stems are slender and somewhat weak, often leaning on surrounding vegetation for support.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, oval seeds with no fluffy parts - they look somewhat like tiny ticks, which gives the genus its "tickseed" nickname. They feel hard and smooth when rolled between your fingers.

habitat: Rose Coreopsis loves wet feet and is found along marsh edges, pond shores, cranberry bogs, and other consistently moist areas in coastal and near-coastal New England. It thrives in sandy or peaty soils that stay damp year-round, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other moisture-loving plants. You're most likely to spot it in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, where it's more common than in other New England states.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small tufts of thread-like leaves in wet areas. The plant is mostly foliage at this time and easily overlooked among other emerging marsh vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from mid to late summer, when the distinctive pink or white flowers appear and make the plant easy to spot against the green marsh backdrop.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue into early fall, followed by seed production. The foliage begins to yellow and becomes less noticeable as the plant prepares for winter.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving little trace above ground. Look for dried seed heads if flowers went to seed before frost.

funFact: Rose Coreopsis is such an oddball that scientists think it might not even be closely related to other pink-flowered coreopsis species - it apparently evolved its rosy petals completely independently, making it one of nature's best examples of "parallel evolution" in the daisy family!
confusionNotes: The pink or white flowers make this nearly impossible to confuse with other coreopsis species, which are all bright yellow. In wet habitats, beginners might mistake it for some type of aster, but asters have many more petals and bloom later in fall.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Rose" Coreopsis, it's not related to actual roses at all - the name just refers to the unusual pink color that's so rare in the tickseed family. This species has a very patchy distribution and is considered uncommon throughout its range, making it a special find for wildflower enthusiasts.
compareHints: Rose Coreopsis is the only tickseed in New England with pink or white petals - all its relatives like Lance-leaved and Whorled Coreopsis have bright yellow flowers. While other coreopsis species often grow in dry, sunny spots, Rose Coreopsis is the wetland specialist of the family. Its thread-like leaves are also much finer than the broader leaves of most other tickseed species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tickseed relatives, Whorled Coreopsis is the only one with thread-like leaves arranged in distinct whorls around the stem.

Lance-leaved Coreopsis differs from other Coreopsis species by its simple, unlobed lance-shaped leaves - Rose Coreopsis has much smaller pink flowers, while Whorled Coreopsis has very finely divided, thread-like leaves.
Plains coreopsis differs from other New England coreopsis species by being an annual (dies each year) rather than perennial, and by having the most deeply divided, feathery leaves of the group.
Tall coreopsis dwarfs all other New England coreopsis species - most relatives like lance-leaved coreopsis and rose coreopsis stay under 3 feet tall.

Among New England's coreopsis species, lobed coreopsis is immediately distinguished by its uniquely shaped leaves - rose coreopsis has narrow linear leaves, lance-leaved has simple spear-shaped leaves, and whorled coreopsis has thread-like leaves in circles around the stem.

Large-flowered tickseed stands out from other New England tickseeds by its size - both the flowers and overall plant are notably larger than rose coreopsis (which has pink flowers) or lance-leaved coreopsis.

Unlike its New England relatives like Lance-leaved Coreopsis (which has simple, narrow leaves) or Rose Coreopsis (which has thin, needle-like leaves), Prairie Coreopsis has those distinctive deeply-divided, finger-like leaves that make it unmistakable.
